Course 16

Intelligence and creativity

What intelligence is, how it is measured, what influences it and how creativity works, without myths.

Lesson 4. Creativity

1 · Lesson

Creativity is usually defined as the ability to produce ideas or products that are both original and useful or appropriate. It is not exclusive to artists: it shows up in cooking, teaching, programming or solving a household problem.

J. P. Guilford distinguished divergent thinking (generating many possibilities) from convergent thinking (choosing the best one). Both are needed. Creativity is linked to openness to experience, deep knowledge of a field and persistence; most important works arrive after years of practice.

The idea that the right hemisphere is "the creative one" is a myth: creativity involves networks across the whole brain. The stereotype of the tormented genius is also doubtful; the relationship between creativity and mental disorders is complex and does not justify romanticising suffering.

2 · Example

Many ideas come when we stop looking for them: in the shower or on a walk. This is the incubation stage described by Graham Wallas in 1926. It works best if the problem has been worked on thoroughly beforehand: the mind keeps combining what it already has.

3 · Activity

Take an everyday object, such as a paper clip or a spoon, and in three minutes write down every use you can think of. Then choose the two most original ones that are also useful. You have just practised divergent and convergent thinking.
